justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I interpreted as a current level near 1,040–1,045, with each successive horizon carrying a slightly higher central expectation. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 1,045 essentially anchors on mean reversion and overnight continuity — absent a major catalyst, prices tend to open near where they closed, with only marginal drift. At one week, the small bump to 1,050 reflects a mild positive carry or trend bias, acknowledging that over several sessions there is slightly more room for directional movement to accumulate. At one month, the 1,065 estimate incorporates a longer-run drift assumption — perhaps tied to modest growth expectations or historical trend — while still remaining close to current levels because one month is short enough that fundamental repricing is unlikely to dominate.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively, as they should, because uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 70-point range (1,010–1,080) reflects typical daily volatility — roughly ±3% — which is consistent with normal realized volatility for many financial instruments. By one week, the interval expands to 125 points, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty plus the possibility that a trending move could develop or reverse. At one month, the 255-point range reflects that macro data releases, central bank decisions, earnings, or geopolitical developments could all accumulate and push the price substantially in either direction, even if the modal outcome remains near current levels.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals entirely. A sudden liquidity shock, surprise policy announcement, or geopolitical escalation could easily produce a move of 5–10% within a single day, breaching the one-day interval. On the upside, a risk-on surge driven by unexpected positive macro data or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty could push prices well above 1,080 intraday. Over the month horizon, a regime change — such as a sustained shift in interest rate expectations or a credit event — could produce a move of 15–20%, placing outcomes near 870 or 1,230, both well outside the stated 90% interval.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals are calibrated under relatively normal market conditions and assume no structural breaks. If volatility itself is currently elevated or suppressed relative to historical norms, the true intervals could be systematically wider or narrower than stated. Tail risks are inherently difficult to price, and the 90% confidence interval by construction leaves a 10% probability mass in the tails — meaning roughly one in ten outcomes should fall outside these bounds even if the model is perfectly calibrated.
